questions.title: Viewing leaf cells
questions.stem: A student observes leaf cells with a light microscope. A drawing of one cell is 36 mm long. The actual cell is 0.09 mm long.

parts.q: Name the structure that contains genetic material and the structure where photosynthesis occurs.
ms: Nucleus (1).
Chloroplast (1).

parts.q: Calculate the magnification of the drawing. Show your working.
ms: Magnification = image size / actual size (1).

parts.q: Describe how to prepare a thin leaf sample on a microscope slide.
ms: Place a thin sample in a drop of water on a slide (1).
Lower a coverslip gently at an angle to reduce trapped air (1).
Remove excess water and begin observing with low-power objective (1).

parts.q: Give three differences between a bacterial cell and a leaf cell.
ms: Bacteria lack a nucleus; leaf cells have one (1).
Bacteria have no chloroplasts; photosynthetic leaf cells have chloroplasts (1).
Bacteria have no mitochondria; leaf cells have mitochondria (1). Accept bacterial circular DNA/plasmids versus chromosomes in a nucleus as an alternative distinct difference.

parts.q: Calculate the increase in mass of the cylinder in water.
Calculate the percentage increase in mass of this cylinder.
Explain why the cylinder in concentrated sugar solution loses mass.
ms: Water moves out of potato cells (1).
Through partially permeable membranes (1).
By osmosis, from a more dilute solution inside to a more concentrated solution outside (1).

parts.q: Describe three controls or improvements that make this comparison more reliable.
ms: Use cylinders of equal dimensions/from the same potato (1).
Use the same immersion time and temperature (1).
Repeat with several cylinders and calculate means; or blot each cylinder consistently before weighing (1).

questions.title: Enzymes and digestion
questions.stem: Amylase digests starch. In a test at 35 °C, starch takes 120 seconds to disappear. At 45 °C it takes 60 seconds.

parts.q: Name the product type made by amylase and the reagent used to test for starch.
ms: Sugars (1).
Iodine solution (1).

parts.q: Calculate the ratio of the time at 35 °C to the time at 45 °C. Give the simplest whole-number ratio.
Explain how bile helps the digestion of fats.
ms: Neutralises stomach acid in the small intestine (1).
Provides alkaline conditions for enzymes (1).
Emulsifies fats into small droplets, increasing surface area for lipase (1).

parts.q: Explain why amylase works very slowly at 80 °C.
ms: High temperature changes the shape of the enzyme/active site (1).
The substrate no longer fits the active site (1).
The enzyme is denatured, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form (1).

questions.title: Transport in the body
questions.stem: Blood circulates between the heart, lungs and body tissues.

parts.q: Name the blood component that carries oxygen and the component involved in clotting.
ms: Red blood cells (1).
Platelets (1).

parts.q: Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle.
ms: Left ventricle pumps blood around the whole body (1).
Needs to generate higher pressure than the right ventricle, which pumps to nearby lungs (1).

parts.q: Explain three features of alveoli that make gas exchange effective.
ms: Large surface area increases exchange (1).
Thin walls provide short diffusion distance (1).
Good blood supply/ventilation maintains a concentration gradient (1).

parts.q: Describe how coronary heart disease develops and one treatment.
ms: Fatty deposits build up in coronary arteries (1).
Reduced blood flow reduces oxygen supply to heart muscle (1).
Stent holds artery open or statins lower blood cholesterol and slow deposit formation (1).

questions.title: Preventing infectious disease
questions.stem: A school has 800 pupils. Following a vaccination programme, 680 pupils are vaccinated.

parts.q: Calculate the percentage of pupils vaccinated.
State one bacterial disease and one viral disease from the course.
ms: Salmonella food poisoning or gonorrhoea (1).
Measles, HIV or tobacco mosaic virus (1).

parts.q: Explain how vaccination reduces the risk of becoming ill after later exposure to a pathogen.
ms: Vaccine introduces dead/inactive pathogen or pathogen antigens.
Antigens stimulate white blood cells.
White blood cells produce specific antibodies.
Some white blood cells remain as memory cells.
On later exposure the specific antibodies are produced faster.
Antibodies destroy the pathogen before it causes serious illness. Accept a valid explanation of reduced transmission protecting unvaccinated people as an alternative final point.
parts.note: Award one mark for each distinct valid linked point, maximum 6.

parts.q: Name the gas in the bubbles and the organelle that absorbs light.
ms: Oxygen (1).
Chloroplast (1).

parts.q: Calculate the decrease in bubbles per minute between 10 cm and 30 cm.
ms: 32 bubbles per minute (1).

parts.q: Explain the pattern in the table.
ms: Light intensity decreases as lamp distance increases (1).
Less light energy is available for photosynthesis (1).
Photosynthesis rate decreases, so fewer oxygen bubbles are produced each minute (1).

parts.q: Suggest three improvements to the method.
ms: Collect gas volume rather than count unequal bubbles (1).
Keep temperature constant using a water bath/heat shield (1).
Repeat each distance and calculate a mean; or control carbon dioxide with the same bicarbonate solution (1).

questions.title: Respiration during exercise
questions.stem: A runner starts a fast sprint. Their muscles need more energy.

parts.q: Complete the word equation for aerobic respiration: glucose + ____ → ____ + water.
ms: Oxygen (1).
Carbon dioxide (1).

parts.q: State two changes to the body during exercise that deliver more oxygen to muscles.
ms: Heart rate increases (1).
Breathing rate and/or depth increases (1).

parts.q: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in human muscles.
ms: Aerobic uses oxygen; anaerobic does not (1).
Anaerobic forms lactic acid; aerobic forms carbon dioxide and water (1).
Anaerobic transfers less energy per glucose molecule (1).

parts.q: Explain why breathing remains fast for a while after the sprint.
ms: Lactic acid accumulated when oxygen supply was insufficient (1).
Extra oxygen is needed to react with/remove accumulated lactic acid (1).
This extra oxygen requirement is the oxygen debt (1).

questions.title: Exchange surfaces and cell size
questions.stem: Model cells are cubes. Cube A has side length 1 mm; cube B has side length 3 mm. Surface area of a cube = 6 × side²; volume = side³.

parts.q: Calculate the surface-area-to-volume ratio of cube B.
ms: Surface area = 6 x 9 = 54 mm² (1).
Volume = 27 mm³ (1).

parts.q: Explain why diffusion alone may be insufficient for a large multicellular organism.
ms: Smaller surface-area-to-volume ratio than a small organism (1).
Longer internal diffusion distances (1).
Diffusion cannot supply all cells rapidly enough to meet demand for oxygen/nutrients (1).

parts.q: A micrograph is 72 mm wide at ×600. Calculate the real width in micrometres.
ms: 120 micrometres (1).

parts.q: Explain how active transport differs from diffusion.
ms: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient; diffusion is down it (1).
Active transport requires energy from respiration; diffusion does not (1).

ms: Zero lies halfway between +2 and -2 (1).
0.35 mol dm⁻³ (1).

ms: Mass loss = 5.50 x 0.07 (1).
Mass loss = 0.385 g (1).

parts.q: Explain why zero net mass change does not mean water molecules have stopped moving.
ms: Water still moves in both directions through the membrane (1).
Equal average rates produce no net transfer (1).

parts.q: Identify a possible systematic error and explain a practical improvement and its benefit.
ms: Valid systematic error such as consistently leaving surface solution on cylinders before weighing (1).
Blot each cylinder using a standard procedure (1).
Reduces bias caused by measuring surface solution rather than tissue mass (1). Accept another coherent error-improvement-benefit sequence.

parts.q: Using rate = 1/time, calculate the reaction rate at pH 7 to 3 significant figures.
Calculate how many times faster the reaction is at pH 7 than at pH 4.
ms: 6 times (1).

parts.q: Explain the effect of pH on enzyme activity.
ms: Changes in pH can alter the active-site shape (1).
Substrate becomes less complementary (1).
Fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form; sufficiently extreme pH can denature the enzyme (1).

parts.q: Explain why temperature, enzyme concentration and starch concentration must each be controlled.
ms: Temperature affects collision rate/denaturation (1).
Enzyme concentration affects the number of available active sites (1).
Starch concentration affects collision frequency/substrate availability, so changes could confound the pH comparison (1).

questions.title: Heart disease and evidence
questions.stem: In a study, 18 of 300 people in group A developed heart disease, compared with 45 of 300 in group B. Group A took part in an exercise programme. The groups were not randomly allocated.

parts.q: Calculate the percentage developing heart disease in group A.
Explain why the study does not prove that exercise alone caused the difference.
ms: Groups may differ in other risk factors such as diet/smoking/age (1).
These confounding factors could explain part/all of the difference (1).

parts.q: Explain how the heart and blood vessels maintain effective delivery of oxygen to body tissues.
ms: Double circulation sends blood to lungs and then to body.
Right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to lungs.
Oxygen enters blood at alveoli.
Left ventricle produces high pressure for circulation to body tissues.
Arteries carry blood away from heart and withstand high pressure.
Capillaries have thin walls enabling short diffusion distance into tissues. Accept valves preventing backflow or red cells carrying oxygen using haemoglobin as alternative relevant points.
parts.note: Award one mark per distinct relevant linked point, maximum 6.

questions.title: Infection and immunity
questions.stem: A viral infection causes symptoms in some patients. A doctor explains that antibiotics will not cure the viral infection.

parts.q: Explain why antibiotics are ineffective against viruses.
ms: Antibiotics target bacterial structures/processes (1).
Viruses reproduce inside host cells and do not have the same targets (1).

parts.q: Describe three ways white blood cells defend the body against pathogens.
ms: Phagocytosis/engulfing pathogens (1).
Producing specific antibodies (1).
Producing antitoxins to neutralise toxins (1).

parts.q: Explain how antibiotic resistance can increase in a bacterial population.
ms: Mutation produces a resistant bacterium/variation already exists (1).
Antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria, leaving resistant bacteria (1).
Resistant bacteria reproduce and pass on resistance, increasing its frequency (1).

parts.q: Give two reasons why a new drug is tested before use in patients.
ms: Determine toxicity/safety (1).
Determine effectiveness or an appropriate dose (1).

questions.title: Limiting photosynthesis
questions.stem: At a fixed temperature, a plant absorbs 2.4 mg of carbon dioxide in 4 minutes at light setting A and 4.8 mg in 4 minutes at setting B. Doubling the light again gives no further increase.

parts.q: Calculate the carbon dioxide uptake rate at setting B.
Calculate the percentage increase in uptake from A to B.
Explain why doubling light beyond B may give no further increase.
ms: Light is no longer the limiting factor (1).
Carbon dioxide concentration or temperature may limit the rate (1).
Increasing that limiting factor, within a suitable range, would allow rate to increase (1).

parts.q: A grower proposes heating the greenhouse all night to increase photosynthesis. Evaluate this proposal.
ms: No photosynthesis without light at night (1).
Heating costs money/energy and may not raise yield enough to cover costs (1).
It may be useful only with lighting and sufficient carbon dioxide, or for preventing cold damage; conclusion must link to conditions (1).

questions.title: Metabolism and exercise
questions.stem: A person runs at increasing speed until oxygen delivery can no longer meet demand.

parts.q: Explain the relationship between respiration and metabolism.
ms: Respiration transfers energy from glucose (1).
This energy supports metabolic reactions such as protein synthesis or conversion of glucose to glycogen (1).

parts.q: Explain why anaerobic respiration leads to muscle fatigue and an oxygen debt.
ms: Glucose is incompletely broken down to lactic acid (1).
Lactic acid accumulation contributes to fatigue (1).
Extra oxygen is required after exercise to react with/remove the lactic acid (1).

parts.q: Describe how lactic acid is processed after exercise.
ms: Transported in blood from muscles to liver (1).
Converted back into glucose in the liver (1).
Oxygen/energy is required during recovery; accept some glucose stored as glycogen (1).

parts.q: Compare anaerobic respiration in yeast with that in muscles.
ms: Yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide; muscles produce lactic acid (1).
Both transfer energy without oxygen/from incomplete breakdown of glucose (1).

questions.title: Reflexes and reaction time
questions.stem: Five ruler-drop distances are 16, 18, 15, 17 and 19 cm.

parts.q: Calculate the mean distance.
ms: Sum = 85 cm (1).

parts.q: Name the type of cell that detects a stimulus and the type of cell that carries an impulse to a muscle.
ms: Receptor (1).
Motor neurone (1).

parts.q: Describe the route taken by an impulse in a reflex arc from a receptor to a muscle.
ms: Sensory neurone carries impulse to central nervous system (1).
Relay neurone passes impulse within CNS (1).
Motor neurone carries impulse to the muscle/effector (1).

parts.q: Explain three controls or improvements in a ruler-drop investigation.
ms: Same starting position/zero aligned with fingers (1).
Same hand/person and posture when comparing conditions (1).
Repeat and calculate mean; avoid cues by varying delay before release (one valid improvement for 1).

questions.title: Blood glucose control
questions.stem: After a meal, blood glucose concentration rises.

parts.q: Name the organ that produces insulin and state how insulin travels to target organs.
ms: Pancreas (1).
In the blood (1).

parts.q: State two effects of insulin that reduce blood glucose concentration.
ms: Glucose moves from blood into cells (1).
Glucose is converted to glycogen in liver/muscles (1).

parts.q: Compare Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes.
ms: Type 1 pancreas produces little/no insulin (1).
Type 2 body cells respond less effectively to insulin (1).
Type 1 often treated with insulin injections; Type 2 often managed with controlled carbohydrate diet and exercise (1).

parts.q: Explain why a person with diabetes should use several blood glucose readings rather than one reading to judge control.
ms: Glucose changes during the day (1).
Meals/exercise affect readings (1).
Several readings reveal patterns and reduce the influence of an unusual reading (1).

questions.title: Hormones and reproduction
questions.stem: Hormones coordinate the menstrual cycle.

parts.q: State where oestrogen is mainly produced and one of its roles in the menstrual cycle.
ms: Ovaries (1).
Builds/thickens uterus lining (1).

parts.q: Name the hormone that causes ovulation and the hormone that stimulates egg maturation.
ms: LH causes ovulation (1).
FSH stimulates egg maturation (1).

parts.q: Explain three ways contraception can prevent pregnancy.
ms: Barrier method: a condom or diaphragm forms a physical barrier.
The barrier prevents sperm reaching the egg, so fertilisation cannot occur.
Hormonal method: an oral contraceptive supplies reproductive hormones.
These can inhibit egg maturation or ovulation, so an egg is not available for fertilisation.
Intrauterine method: an IUD is placed inside the uterus. Accept sterilisation blocking sperm ducts or oviducts as an alternative method.

The IUD can prevent implantation, impair sperm/fertilisation, or release hormones that thicken cervical mucus. For sterilisation: gametes cannot meet. Award this explanation mark only with the matching method. Do not credit abortion as contraception.
parts.note: Award up to 2 marks for each of three distinct methods; maximum 6.

questions.title: Inheritance of a recessive condition
questions.stem:

parts.q: State the meaning of allele and genotype.
ms: Allele is a version of a gene (1).
Genotype is the combination of alleles an individual has (1).

parts.q: Complete Box A and Box B in the provided Punnett square.
ms: Box A = Dd (1).
Box B = Dd (1).

parts.q: Calculate the probability of an offspring having the condition. Give a percentage.
ms: Only dd has the condition; 1 of 4 (1).

parts.q: Explain why a dominant allele can be expressed in a heterozygous person, and why this does not mean it is always common in a population.
ms: Heterozygous means two different alleles (1).
One copy of a dominant allele is sufficient to affect phenotype (1).
Dominance describes expression, not how frequent an allele is (1).
Frequency also depends on inheritance, selection and chance/population history (1).

questions.title: Selection and biodiversity
questions.stem: Some beetles are green and some are brown. Birds find green beetles more easily on dark soil.

parts.q: State what is meant by variation and name one environmental cause of variation.
ms: Differences between individuals of a species (1).
Diet/light/exercise or another valid environmental factor (1).

parts.q: Explain how the proportion of brown beetles could increase over many generations.
ms: There is inherited variation in colour (1).
Brown beetles are less likely to be eaten (1).
More survive to reproduce (1).
They pass alleles for brown colour to offspring, increasing frequency (1).

parts.q: Give two reasons why a species may become extinct.
ms: Environmental change/habitat loss/new predator (one for 1).
New disease/competition/catastrophic event (a second distinct reason for 1).

parts.q: State two benefits of maintaining biodiversity.
ms: Helps maintain stable ecosystems/interdependence (1).
Preserves genetic resources/food/medicines or other valid ecosystem service (1).

questions.title: Sampling a field
questions.stem: Ten randomly placed quadrats each cover 0.25 m². A total of 60 daisies are counted. The field has area 200 m².

parts.q: Calculate the total area sampled.
Estimate the number of daisies in the field.
ms: Mean density = 60 / 2.5 (1).
24 daisies/m² (1).

parts.q: Describe how to place quadrats randomly.
ms: Set up numbered coordinates across the field (1).
Use random numbers to select positions (1).

parts.q: Explain two limitations of this estimate.
ms: Daisies may be unevenly distributed (1).
Small sampled fraction may not represent the whole field (1).
Counting/identification or seasonal differences can affect the estimate (1).

questions.title: Material cycles
questions.stem: Microorganisms break down dead leaves in a woodland. Water and carbon are continually recycled.

parts.q: Name the process by which plants remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and the process by which decomposers release it.
ms: Photosynthesis (1).
Respiration (1).

parts.q: Describe how water from the sea can return to the sea after falling on a woodland.
ms: Water evaporates from the sea and condenses to form clouds (1).
Precipitation/rain falls onto the woodland (1).
Water returns by surface runoff/rivers or groundwater flow (1).

parts.q: Describe how carbon from a leaf can return to a new tree.
ms: Decomposers break down leaf material (1).
Respiration releases carbon dioxide to atmosphere (1).
New tree absorbs carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, building biomass (1).

parts.q: Suggest two actions that reduce human impacts on biodiversity.
ms: Protect/restore habitats, such as reforestation (1).
Reduce pollution/waste, conservation breeding, or sustainable resource use (a second valid action for 1).

parts.q: Calculate the percentage increase in mean reaction time with distraction.
ms: Means 220 ms and 280 ms (1).

parts.q: Explain how an impulse crosses a synapse.
ms: Impulse triggers release of a neurotransmitter (1).
Chemical diffuses across gap (1).
Binds to receptors on next neurone and triggers a new electrical impulse (1).

parts.q: Compare nervous and hormonal coordination.
ms: Nervous signals travel along neurones; hormones are carried in blood (1).
Nervous responses generally faster/shorter lasting and more localised; hormonal responses generally slower/longer lasting (1).

parts.q: Suggest two ways to improve the validity of this comparison.
ms: Test same people in both conditions with order randomised (1).
Control sleep/caffeine/practice and other distractions, or use more participants (1).

questions.title: Negative feedback
questions.stem: A fasting person has falling blood glucose concentration. For the thyroxine question, use this information: the pituitary releases TSH, which stimulates the thyroid gland to release thyroxine.

parts.q: Explain how glucagon restores blood glucose concentration.
ms: Pancreas detects low blood glucose/releases glucagon (1).
Glucagon travels to liver in blood (1).
Stimulates conversion of glycogen to glucose (1).
Glucose released into blood raises concentration (1).

parts.q: Explain why this is negative feedback.
ms: Response opposes the initial fall (1).
As concentration returns to normal, stimulation/glucagon secretion decreases (1).

parts.q: Explain how adrenaline prepares the body for action.
ms: Increases heart rate (1).
Increases delivery of oxygen and glucose to muscles for increased respiration (1).

parts.q: Explain how thyroxine secretion is controlled when its concentration becomes too high.
ms: High thyroxine inhibits pituitary release of TSH (1).
Less TSH stimulates thyroid, reducing thyroxine secretion (1).

questions.title: Reproductive hormone interactions
questions.stem: A clinic treats some cases of infertility with hormones. Success is not guaranteed.

parts.q: State the roles of FSH and LH during fertility treatment.
ms: FSH stimulates maturation of eggs (1).
LH stimulates ovulation/release of an egg (1).

parts.q: Explain how oestrogen and progesterone help regulate the menstrual cycle.
ms: Oestrogen stimulates rebuilding uterus lining (1).
Oestrogen inhibits FSH and stimulates LH release (1).
Progesterone maintains uterus lining (1).
Progesterone inhibits FSH and LH (1).

parts.q: A clinic reports 72 births from 240 treatment cycles. Calculate its birth rate per treatment cycle as a percentage.
Give one benefit and one risk or disadvantage of IVF.
ms: Can enable an infertile couple to have a child (1).
Multiple births/hormone side effects/emotional or financial cost; one valid disadvantage (1).

questions.title: Meiosis and inheritance
questions.stem: A recessive allele a causes a genetic condition. A carrier Aa has a child with a person aa who has the condition.

parts.q: Use a genetic cross to find the probability of a child having the condition. Give a decimal probability.
ms: Carrier gametes A and a; affected parent gamete a (1).
Offspring Aa and aa in equal proportions (1).
Probability 1/2 or 50% (1).

parts.q: Explain how meiosis and fertilisation maintain chromosome number across generations.
ms: Meiosis halves chromosome number in gametes (1).
Fertilisation joins/fuses two gamete nuclei (1).
Restores the full chromosome number in the zygote (1).

parts.q: Explain why siblings can have different phenotypes even with the same parents.
ms: Sexual reproduction produces different combinations of parental alleles (1).
Environmental differences can also affect phenotype (1).

parts.q: Evaluate using the result of this cross to predict the outcomes for exactly two children.
ms: Probability applies independently to each conception (1).
It does not guarantee that exactly one of two children will have the condition (1).

questions.title: Antibiotic resistance and genetic engineering
questions.stem: A hospital finds that an increasing proportion of bacteria are resistant to an antibiotic.

parts.q: Explain how resistance becomes more common and how prescribing decisions can slow this process.
ms: Random mutation creates an allele giving resistance/variation already exists.
Antibiotic creates a selection pressure.
Susceptible bacteria are killed.
Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce rapidly.
Resistance allele is passed to offspring, increasing its frequency.
Prescribing antibiotics only when needed reduces selection pressure. Accept completion of the prescribed course as an alternative control, with a correct explanation.
parts.note: Award one mark per distinct valid linked point, maximum 6.

parts.q: Describe how bacteria can be genetically engineered to produce human insulin.
ms: Human insulin gene is isolated using enzymes (1).
Gene inserted into a vector/plasmid using enzymes (1).
Vector introduces gene into bacteria (1).
Modified bacteria are grown and express the gene to produce insulin, which is collected/purified (1).

questions.title: Interdependence and sampling
questions.stem: A field has area 800 m². Twenty 0.5 m² quadrats contain a total of 150 clover plants. Fewer clover plants are found near a shaded hedge.

parts.q: Estimate the total number of clover plants in the field.
ms: Area sampled = 20 x 0.5 = 10 m² (1).
Density = 150/10 = 15 plants/m² (1).
Estimate = 15 x 800 = 12000 plants (1).

parts.q: Design an investigation of the effect of distance from the hedge on clover abundance.
ms: Place a tape/transect perpendicular to hedge (1).
Sample quadrats at regular measured distances (1).
Count clover using a consistent inclusion rule and record light intensity/other relevant factor (1).
Repeat parallel transects and calculate mean abundance at each distance (1).

parts.q: Explain why the association with shade does not prove that light is the only cause.
ms: Other factors may vary with distance (1).
For example water/mineral availability/trampling/competition (1).
Need control or additional measurement/manipulation of these variables to test causation (1).

questions.title: Carbon and water cycles
questions.stem: A restoration project plants 400 trees. In a simplified model, each tree removes an average of 12 kg carbon dioxide per year. In practice, the value varies with tree age and environmental conditions.

parts.q: Calculate the total carbon dioxide removed per year in this model.
ms: 4800 kg per year (1).

parts.q: Explain how carbon from dead leaves can return to the atmosphere.
ms: Microorganisms/decomposers break down dead material (1).
Their respiration releases carbon dioxide (1).

parts.q: Explain how water is continually recycled between the sea, atmosphere and land.
ms: Evaporation from sea/land and transpiration from plants move water into air (1).
Water vapour condenses into clouds and falls as precipitation (1).
Runoff/rivers/groundwater return water to the sea (1).

parts.q: Explain how deforestation can increase atmospheric carbon dioxide.
ms: Fewer trees remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis (1).
Burning felled trees releases carbon dioxide (1).
Decay/respiration of dead biomass also releases carbon dioxide (1).

questions.title: Atoms and the periodic table
questions.topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
questions.stem: An atom of sodium has atomic number 11 and mass number 23.

parts.q: State the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in this atom.
ms: 11 protons (1).
23 - 11 = 12 neutrons (1).
11 electrons (1).

parts.q: Give the electronic structure of sodium and use it to identify its group.
ms: Group 1, because it has one electron in its outer shell (1).

parts.q: Explain how a sodium ion forms.
ms: Sodium atom loses one electron (1).
Forms Na⁺, a positive ion with charge +1 (1).

parts.q: Describe and explain the trend in reactivity down Group 1.
ms: Reactivity increases down the group (1).
Outer electron is farther from nucleus/more shielded (1).
Outer electron is more easily lost (1).

questions.title: Structures and properties
questions.stem: Sodium chloride is an ionic compound. Carbon dioxide consists of small molecules.

parts.q: Calculate the relative formula mass of sodium chloride, NaCl. Use Aᵣ: Na = 23, Cl = 35.5.
Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity but molten sodium chloride does.
ms: Solid ions are held in fixed positions (1).
Molten ions are free to move (1).
Moving ions carry charge (1).

parts.q: Explain why carbon dioxide has a much lower boiling point than sodium chloride.
ms: Weak forces between carbon dioxide molecules (1).
Less energy needed to overcome these than the strong electrostatic attractions between ions (1).
Boiling carbon dioxide separates molecules; it does not break covalent bonds within them (1).

parts.q: State two properties of most metals that make them useful for electrical wiring.
ms: Good electrical conductors (1).
Ductile/can be drawn into wires (1).

questions.title: Mass and solution concentration
questions.stem: A student dissolves 12 g of sodium chloride in water to make 300 cm³ of solution. A separate reaction uses 5.0 g of magnesium and 3.2 g of oxygen to form only magnesium oxide.

parts.q: Convert 300 cm³ to dm³.
ms: Divide by 1000 (1).

parts.q: Calculate the solution concentration in g/dm³. Use concentration = mass / volume.
ms: Concentration = 12/0.300 (1).
Correct unit g/dm³ (1).

parts.q: Calculate the mass of magnesium oxide formed if all reactants react.
Explain why heating a metal in an open container can increase its mass without breaking conservation of mass.
ms: Metal reacts with oxygen (1).
Oxygen enters from the air and becomes part of the solid (1).
Total mass of metal plus oxygen is conserved when the whole system is considered (1).

questions.title: Reactivity and extraction
questions.stem: Iron oxide is heated with carbon. A different metal, aluminium, is more reactive than carbon. From 80 tonnes of ore, a process collects 24 tonnes of iron.

parts.q: Calculate the percentage of the ore mass collected as iron.
ms: Percentage = mass of iron collected / mass of ore x 100 (1).

parts.q: Explain why carbon can extract iron from iron oxide but cannot extract aluminium from aluminium oxide.
ms: Carbon is more reactive than iron, so removes oxygen from iron oxide (1).
Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot remove oxygen from aluminium oxide (1).

parts.q: Describe what happens when magnesium is added to copper sulfate solution.
ms: Copper forms as a brown/pink solid (1).
Blue colour fades as copper ions are removed (1).
Magnesium displaces copper because magnesium is more reactive (1).

parts.q: State what oxidation and reduction mean in terms of oxygen.
ms: Oxidation is gain of oxygen (1).
Reduction is loss of oxygen (1).

questions.title: Making a soluble salt
questions.stem: A student makes copper sulfate crystals using dilute sulfuric acid and copper oxide.

parts.q: Name the products of a reaction between an acid and a metal oxide.
ms: Salt (1).
Water (1).

parts.q: Describe how to make pure, dry copper sulfate crystals from these starting materials.
ms: Warm dilute sulfuric acid gently using suitable safe heating; wear eye protection.
Add copper oxide in small portions while stirring.
Continue adding until solid remains/no more reacts, showing excess oxide.
Filter to remove excess unreacted copper oxide.
Heat filtrate gently to evaporate some water, then allow to cool so crystals form.
Filter crystals and dry between filter papers/in a warm place. Do not credit boiling to dryness.
parts.note: Award one mark per distinct valid step, maximum 6.

parts.q: Explain why an excess of copper oxide is added and then filtered off.
ms: Ensures all acid is reacted/neutralised (1).
Insoluble excess oxide can be removed, leaving a solution without excess acid (1).

questions.title: Electrolysis
questions.stem: Molten lead bromide contains Pb²⁺ and Br⁻ ions. Electrodes are connected to a direct-current supply.

parts.q: State which electrode attracts Pb²⁺ ions and which attracts Br⁻ ions.
ms: Pb²⁺ attracted to negative cathode (1).
Br⁻ attracted to positive anode (1).

parts.q: Explain why electrolysis requires molten lead bromide rather than solid lead bromide.
ms: Ions must be able to move to electrodes (1).
Ions in solid are fixed in place; molten ions can move (1).

parts.q: Name the products at the two electrodes.
ms: Lead at cathode (1).
Bromine at anode (1).

parts.q: Explain why aluminium extraction is energy intensive and give two ways to reduce its environmental impact.
ms: Large electrical energy input needed for electrolysis (1).
Electricity from fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide (1).
Recycle aluminium to reduce need for extraction (1).
Use electricity from low-carbon sources/improve energy efficiency (1).

questions.title: Energy changes in reactions
questions.stem: In an insulated cup, 25 cm³ of acid reacts with 25 cm³ of alkali. Temperature rises from 19.5 °C to 27.0 °C.

parts.q: Calculate the temperature rise.
State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic and explain your answer.
ms: Exothermic (1).
Transfers energy to surroundings, increasing temperature (1).

parts.q: Describe three precautions that improve the temperature measurement.
ms: Use an insulated cup with lid (1).
Stir so temperature is uniform (1).
Record the highest temperature promptly/use a temperature probe; same starting temperatures for both solutions (1).

parts.q: Describe an energy profile for this exothermic reaction.
ms: Reactant energy level above product energy level (1).
Curve rises to a peak then falls to products (1).
Activation energy from reactant level to peak; overall energy change downward (1).

title: Chemistry Paper 1 — Higher · Original practice
subject: Chemistry
coverage: Atomic structure and the periodic table

questions.title: Isotopes and electronic structure
questions.topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
questions.stem: A sample of element X contains 75% atoms of mass 35 and 25% atoms of mass 37. Every atom of X has 17 protons.

parts.q: Calculate the relative atomic mass of X.
ms: Weighted contribution 0.75 x 35 (1).

parts.q: Explain why these two atom types are isotopes.
ms: Same number of protons/atomic number (1).
Different numbers of neutrons/mass numbers (1).

parts.q: Give the electronic structure of X and explain the charge on its usual ion.
ms: Gains one electron for a full outer shell (1).
Forms X⁻ with charge -1 (1).

parts.q: Explain why chlorine is more reactive than bromine.
ms: Chlorine has fewer shells/less shielding so incoming electron is closer to nucleus (1).
Stronger attraction means chlorine gains an electron more readily (1).

questions.title: Comparing giant structures
questions.stem: Diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide have giant covalent structures.

parts.q: Explain why diamond is hard and has a high melting point.
ms: Each carbon forms four covalent bonds (1).
Bonds form a rigid three-dimensional network (1).
Many strong covalent bonds require much energy to break (1).

parts.q: Explain why graphite conducts electricity and is slippery.
ms: Each carbon has three covalent bonds, leaving delocalised electrons (1).
Electrons can move and carry charge (1).
Weak forces between layers allow layers to slide (1).

parts.q: Calculate the relative formula mass of SiO₂. Use Aᵣ: Si = 28, O = 16.
Explain why a small molecule such as methane has a lower melting point than silicon dioxide.
ms: Only weak intermolecular forces need overcoming in methane (1).
Strong covalent bonds throughout silicon dioxide require much more energy to break (1).

questions.title: Moles and reacting masses
questions.stem: Magnesium reacts: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Use Aᵣ: Mg = 24, O = 16. A 6.0 g sample of magnesium is completely burned in excess oxygen.

parts.q: Calculate the amount of magnesium in moles.
Calculate the mass of magnesium oxide formed.
ms: Mg:MgO mole ratio 1:1, so 0.25 mol MgO (1).
Mᵣ MgO = 40 (1).

parts.q: Calculate the mass of oxygen that reacts.
A second experiment gives a lower measured solid mass than predicted. Suggest one experimental cause and explain why it gives a lower value. Explain why this is not failure of conservation of mass.
ms: Some magnesium oxide escapes as smoke/product is lost (1).
Escaped product is not included in measured solid mass (1).
Total mass including escaped substances remains conserved (1).

questions.title: Limiting reactants
questions.stem: 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. A mixture contains 0.30 mol NaOH and 0.20 mol H₂SO₄. Use Mᵣ: Na₂SO₄ = 142.

parts.q: Identify the limiting reactant and justify your answer quantitatively.
ms: 0.30 mol NaOH requires 0.15 mol H₂SO₄ (1).
0.20 mol acid is available, so acid is in excess (1).
NaOH is the limiting reactant (1).

parts.q: Calculate the mass of sodium sulfate formed.
ms: 2:1 ratio gives 0.15 mol Na₂SO₄ (1).

parts.q: Calculate the amount of sulfuric acid left after reaction.
Explain why doubling only the amount of acid does not double the mass of salt formed.
ms: NaOH remains limiting (1).
No additional NaOH is available to form more salt (1).

questions.title: Acids and electrolysis
questions.stem: An aqueous solution of copper chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes.

parts.q: Predict the products and explain why they form at each electrode.
ms: Copper at negative cathode (1).
Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper ions are discharged (1).
Chlorine at positive anode (1).
Halide ions are present, so chlorine forms rather than oxygen (1).

parts.q: Write the cathode half-equation and identify whether this is oxidation or reduction.
ms: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; correct reactants including 2 electrons (1).
Correct product/charge balance (1).
Reduction because electrons are gained (1).

parts.q: Explain the difference between a concentrated acid and a strong acid.
ms: Concentration is the amount of dissolved acid per volume (1).
Strength describes the extent of ionisation in aqueous solution (1).
A strong acid is completely ionised, whereas a weak acid is only partly ionised (1).

questions.title: Preparing a salt safely
questions.stem: A technician needs crystals of zinc sulfate from zinc oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.

parts.q: Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction.
ms: ZnO + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂O; correct formulas (1).
Balanced with all coefficients 1 (1).

parts.q: Describe a safe procedure that produces pure, dry zinc sulfate crystals. Explain important steps.
ms: Wear eye protection and warm dilute acid gently without boiling.
Add zinc oxide with stirring until some remains, ensuring all acid reacts.
Filter to remove excess insoluble zinc oxide.
Gently evaporate some water to concentrate the filtrate.
Allow solution to cool for crystals to form; do not heat to dryness.
Filter crystals and dry them between filter papers/in a warm place.
parts.note: Award one mark per distinct valid step/explanation, maximum 6.

parts.q: Explain why zinc metal could also make zinc sulfate but would need an extra safety precaution.
ms: Zinc reacts with acid to release hydrogen (1).
Hydrogen is flammable, so avoid naked flames/ignition sources (1).

questions.title: Bond energies and reaction profiles
questions.stem: For H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl, bond energies are H–H = 436 kJ/mol, Cl–Cl = 242 kJ/mol and H–Cl = 431 kJ/mol.

parts.q: Calculate the energy needed to break the reactant bonds per mole of reaction.
Calculate the overall energy change per mole of reaction.
ms: Energy released making bonds = 2 x 431 = 862 kJ/mol (1).
Change = energy in - energy out = 678 - 862 (1).

parts.q: Explain why the reaction is exothermic in terms of bonds.
ms: Bond breaking absorbs energy and bond making releases energy (1).
More energy is released making product bonds than absorbed breaking reactant bonds (1).

parts.q: Explain how a catalyst changes the reaction profile and overall energy change.
ms: Provides alternative reaction pathway (1).
Lower activation energy/lower peak (1).
Reactant and product energy levels/overall energy change are unchanged (1).

title: Chemistry Paper 2 — Foundation · Original practice

Calculate the mean rate from 20 seconds to 60 seconds.

parts.q: Explain why gas volume stops increasing after 60 seconds.
ms: Reaction has finished (1).
A reactant has been used up/limiting reactant exhausted (1).

parts.q: Explain why smaller pieces of the same total mass of a solid react faster with acid.
ms: Greater total surface area (1).
More solid particles exposed to acid (1).
More frequent successful collisions each second (1).

questions.title: Investigating concentration
questions.topic: Rate and extent of chemical change
questions.stem: A student reacts magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid and collects hydrogen in a gas syringe.

parts.q: State the test for hydrogen and the positive result.
ms: Apply a lit splint to a small sample (1).
Squeaky pop (1).

parts.q: Plan an investigation of how acid concentration affects the initial rate. Include controls and safety.
ms: Use a range of measured acid concentrations of equal volume.
Use identical magnesium mass/length and cleaned surface.
Keep temperature constant.
Connect an airtight flask to gas syringe and start timing promptly on mixing.
Measure gas volume at short fixed intervals; compare volume/time or initial slopes.
Repeat each concentration and calculate means; wear eye protection and keep hydrogen away from flames. Safety must be included for full 6 marks.
parts.note: Award one mark per distinct valid point, maximum 6.

parts.q: Explain why adding a catalyst can make a reaction faster.
ms: Provides a pathway with lower activation energy (1).
More collisions have sufficient energy to react (1).

questions.title: Crude oil and fuels
questions.stem: A fuel molecule is propane, C₃H₈. Complete combustion is C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Use Aᵣ: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16.

parts.q: Calculate the relative formula mass of propane.
Calculate the relative formula mass of carbon dioxide.
Explain how fractional distillation separates crude oil.
ms: Oil is heated/vaporised and enters a column with a temperature gradient (1).
Hydrocarbons have different boiling points (1).
Fractions condense at different heights/temperatures (1).

parts.q: Describe three trends as hydrocarbon chain length increases.
ms: Boiling point increases (1).
Viscosity increases (1).
Flammability decreases (1).

questions.title: Cracking hydrocarbons
questions.stem: Large hydrocarbon molecules can be cracked. One reaction is C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄.

parts.q: State why cracking is useful.
ms: Produces smaller hydrocarbons that are useful fuels (1).
Produces alkenes used to make polymers/other useful chemicals (1).

parts.q: State the conditions for catalytic cracking.
ms: Vaporise hydrocarbons and heat to a high temperature (1).
Pass vapour over a hot catalyst (1).

parts.q: Name the test that distinguishes ethene from an alkane and give the positive result for ethene.
ms: Add/shake with bromine water (1).
Orange bromine water becomes colourless with ethene (1).

parts.q: Explain how bromine water distinguishes the cracked alkene from an alkane, and explain why cracking is a chemical change.
ms: The alkene decolourises bromine water.
The alkane does not decolourise bromine water under the test conditions.
Bonds are broken and new bonds are formed during cracking.
New substances with different molecules are produced.

questions.title: Chromatography
questions.stem: A spot moves 3.6 cm from the baseline while the solvent front moves 6.0 cm. A chromatogram of a different sample shows three separate spots.

parts.q: Calculate the Rf value of the first spot.
ms: Distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent (1).

parts.q: Explain why the baseline is drawn in pencil and above the solvent surface.
ms: Pencil does not dissolve/run with solvent (1).
Above surface prevents sample dissolving directly into solvent reservoir (1).

parts.q: State what three spots suggest and explain why comparing Rf values requires the same solvent.
ms: Sample is a mixture/contains at least three substances (1).
Substances have different attractions/solubilities in different solvents (1).
Their travel distances/Rf values therefore depend on solvent (1).

parts.q: Describe the test for carbon dioxide and its positive result.
ms: Collect/pass gas into limewater (1).
Bubble the gas through it (1).
Limewater becomes milky/cloudy (1).

questions.title: Our atmosphere
questions.stem: In a simplified model, 1000 cm³ of dry air contains 780 cm³ nitrogen and 210 cm³ oxygen.

parts.q: Calculate the percentage of the air that is oxygen.
Calculate the total volume of gases other than nitrogen and oxygen.
Explain how photosynthesis changed the early atmosphere.
ms: Algae/plants used carbon dioxide (1).
Released oxygen (1).
Carbon became stored in biomass/fossil fuels, contributing to falling atmospheric carbon dioxide (1).

parts.q: Explain how increased carbon dioxide contributes to warming.
ms: Earth emits infrared radiation (1).
Carbon dioxide absorbs some outgoing infrared (1).
Re-emits radiation, reducing net energy loss and warming surface/lower atmosphere (1).

questions.title: Water and resources
questions.stem: A treatment works takes in 5000 litres of water and supplies 4200 litres of potable water. An alternative desalination process uses much more electrical energy.

parts.q: Calculate the percentage of input water supplied as potable water.
Describe how fresh water is treated to make it potable.
ms: Choose a suitable fresh-water source (1).
Filter to remove solid particles (1).
Sterilise using chlorine/ozone/ultraviolet to kill microorganisms (1).

parts.q: Explain why potable water is not necessarily pure water.
ms: Potable means safe to drink (1).
Can contain safe levels of dissolved substances/minerals (1).

parts.q: Evaluate using desalination instead of fresh-water treatment in a dry coastal area.
ms: Seawater provides a plentiful local water source (1).
Distillation/reverse osmosis requires substantial energy/cost (1).
Reasoned judgement balancing limited fresh water against energy/environmental impacts (1).

title: Chemistry Paper 2 — Higher · Original practice
subject: Chemistry
coverage: Rate and extent of chemical change

questions.title: Rates from data
questions.topic: Rate and extent of chemical change
questions.stem: A tangent to a gas-volume curve at 30 s passes through (10 s, 22 cm³) and (50 s, 62 cm³). The final volume is 90 cm³ after 120 s.

parts.q: Calculate the instantaneous rate at 30 s using the tangent.
ms: Change in volume = 62 - 22 = 40 cm³ (1).
Change in time = 50 - 10 = 40 s (1).
Gradient = 1.0 cm³/s (1).

parts.q: Calculate the mean rate over the whole 120 s.
Explain why the instantaneous rate is higher than the overall mean.
ms: Reactant concentration decreases as reaction proceeds (1).
Fewer successful collisions per second later in reaction lower the mean (1).

parts.q: Explain the effect of increasing temperature on reaction rate.
ms: Particles move faster/have greater kinetic energy (1).
Collisions are more frequent (1).
A greater fraction of collisions have energy at least equal to activation energy (1).

questions.title: Reversible reactions and equilibrium
questions.topic: Rate and extent of chemical change
questions.stem: A sealed system reaches equilibrium for A(g) + B(g) ⇌ C(g). The forward reaction is exothermic. Initially, equilibrium contains 0.60 mol C. After a change, it contains 0.45 mol C.

parts.q: Calculate the percentage decrease in amount of C.
Explain what is meant by dynamic equilibrium in this system.
ms: Closed system with no matter entering/leaving (1).
Forward and reverse reactions continue (1).
Equal rates keep concentrations constant, not necessarily equal (1).

parts.q: Predict and explain how increasing temperature affects the equilibrium amount of C.
ms: Amount of C decreases (1).
Equilibrium shifts in endothermic/reverse direction (1).
This opposes the temperature increase (1).

parts.q: Predict and explain the effect of increasing pressure on the equilibrium position.
ms: Shifts to C/right (1).
Right side has fewer gas molecules, opposing pressure rise (1).

questions.title: Fuels and cracking
questions.stem: A hydrocarbon fuel is C₆H₁₄. In a complete combustion experiment, 8.6 g of fuel produces 26.4 g CO₂. Use Aᵣ: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16.

parts.q: Write a balanced equation for complete combustion of C₆H₁₄ using whole-number coefficients.
ms: Correct formulas C₆H₁₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O (1).
Carbon/hydrogen balance gives 6CO₂ and 7H₂O per fuel molecule (1).
2C₆H₁₄ + 19O₂ → 12CO₂ + 14H₂O (1).

parts.q: Calculate the mass of CO₂ made per gram of fuel in this experiment.
ms: 3.07 g CO₂ per g fuel; accept 3.1 (1).

parts.q: Explain why incomplete combustion is dangerous.
ms: Forms carbon monoxide (1).
Toxic because it reduces blood ability to carry oxygen (1).

parts.q: Explain how cracking changes the usefulness and composition of a long-chain alkane feedstock.
ms: Breaks large molecules into smaller molecules by thermal decomposition (1).
Produces shorter-chain fuel alkanes (1).
Produces alkenes with C=C bonds used as chemical feedstocks/making polymers (1).

Evaluate the claim that the mixture contains only P and Q.
ms: Spots at 24 and 52 mm match P and Q under these conditions (1).
Third spot suggests at least one additional substance (1).
Matching Rf supports identity but is not definitive; different substances may share an Rf (1).

parts.q: Explain separation in paper chromatography in terms of the two phases.
ms: Paper is stationary phase; solvent is mobile phase (1).
Different substances distribute differently between phases/have different solubilities and attractions (1).
Substances with stronger attraction to mobile phase move farther (1).

parts.q: A formulated product contains several components. Explain why a formulation can still have consistent properties.
ms: Components are chosen in carefully measured proportions (1).
Their combined properties are designed for a particular purpose (1).

questions.title: Atmospheric chemistry
questions.stem: A manufacturer emits 24000 tonnes CO₂ per year. A change cuts emissions by 15%. Burning its fuel can also produce sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particulates.

parts.q: Calculate the new annual CO₂ emissions.
ms: Reduction = 0.15 x 24000 = 3600 tonnes (1).
20400 tonnes/year (1).

parts.q: Explain how sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides arise during combustion.
ms: Sulfur impurities in fuel burn to form sulfur dioxide (1).
Nitrogen and oxygen from air react (1).
High engine/furnace temperatures enable their reaction (1).

parts.q: Describe two environmental or health effects of these pollutants, other than enhanced greenhouse warming.
ms: Sulfur dioxide/nitrogen oxides cause acid rain/respiratory problems (1).
Particulates cause respiratory harm/global dimming (1).

parts.q: Explain why uncertainty in climate predictions does not mean increasing greenhouse gases have no effect.
ms: Models contain uncertainties about future emissions/complex interactions (1).
Physical absorption of infrared and multiple lines of evidence still support a warming effect (1).

questions.title: Treating water
questions.stem: A town considers a freshwater plant and a reverse-osmosis desalination plant. Freshwater treatment uses 0.60 kWh per m³; desalination uses 3.6 kWh per m³. Each must supply 12000 m³ per day.

parts.q: Calculate the extra daily electrical energy used by desalination.
ms: Extra energy per m³ = 3.6 - 0.60 = 3.0 kWh (1).
36000 kWh per day (1).

parts.q: Explain how reverse osmosis produces potable water from seawater.
ms: Seawater is forced through membranes (1).
High pressure is applied (1).
Membranes allow water through but remove most dissolved salts (1).

parts.q: Describe the main stages of sewage treatment.
ms: Screening/grit removal removes large solids (1).
Sedimentation separates sludge from effluent (1).
Anaerobic digestion treats sludge (1).
Aerobic biological treatment treats liquid effluent (1).

questions.title: Choosing materials over a life cycle
questions.stem: A retailer compares a single-use glass bottle with a reusable plastic bottle. The plastic bottle is reused 20 times, but washing uses energy and water.

parts.q: State two stages, other than manufacture, considered in a life cycle assessment.
ms: Raw material extraction/processing (1).
Transport/use/disposal or recycling (a second distinct stage for 1).

parts.q: Explain how recycling a metal reduces demand for finite resources.
ms: Recovered metal replaces metal from newly mined ore (1).
Reduces extraction and associated waste/energy demand (1).

parts.q: Evaluate the claim that the reusable plastic bottle must always have less environmental impact than glass. Use a life-cycle approach.
ms: Consider energy/materials needed to extract raw materials and manufacture both bottles.
Plastic may be lighter, reducing transport energy.
Glass and plastic have different recycling options and disposal impacts.
Repeated use shares manufacturing impacts across many uses.
Washing adds water, detergent and energy use each time.
A justified conclusion depends on actual reuse, transport, energy sources and disposal data; no universal winner without quantities. Credit other valid linked factors, not unsupported slogans.
parts.note: Award one mark per distinct reasoned point, maximum 6.

questions.title: Energy on a playground
questions.stem: A 30 kg child travels at 4.0 m/s and is then lifted 1.5 m vertically. Take gravitational field strength g = 10 N/kg. Use Eₖ = 0.5mv² and Eₚ = mgh.

parts.q: Calculate the kinetic energy at 4.0 m/s.
ms: Speed squared = 16 (1).

parts.q: Calculate the increase in gravitational potential energy when lifted.
ms: Correct multiplication (1).

parts.q: Describe the energy transfers as the child slides down a rough slide.
ms: Gravitational potential store decreases and kinetic store initially increases (1).
Friction transfers energy to thermal stores of child/slide/surroundings (1).

parts.q: Explain why the total energy is still conserved even when the slide becomes warm.
ms: Energy is transferred between stores, not destroyed (1).
Thermal energy spreads to surroundings and becomes less useful for further transfers (1).

questions.title: Heating water
questions.stem: A heater transfers 42000 J to 0.50 kg of water. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/(kg °C). Use E = mcΔθ.

parts.q: Calculate the temperature rise of the water.
ms: Temperature rise = 42000/(0.50 x 4200) (1).
20 degrees Celsius (1).

parts.q: The transfer takes 100 s. Calculate the mean power transferred to the water. Use P = E/t.
Describe a safe method to determine the specific heat capacity of water. Include the measurements, calculation and how to reduce energy loss.
ms: Measure the mass of water with a balance.
Measure its initial temperature using a thermometer or temperature probe.
Use an immersion heater with a measured energy input from a joulemeter, or measured power and time.
Stir the water and measure its temperature rise after heating.
Calculate c = E/(mass x temperature rise).
Insulate the container and use a lid; keep electrical connections dry and handle hot water carefully. Safety and an energy-loss precaution are both needed for full 6 marks.
parts.note: Award one mark per distinct valid point, maximum 6.

questions.title: Current and charge
questions.stem: A lamp has current 0.40 A and potential difference 6.0 V. It is on for 50 s. Use Q = It, E = QV and P = VI.

parts.q: Calculate the charge passing through the lamp.
Calculate the energy transferred to the lamp.
Calculate the power of the lamp.
Describe how to connect an ammeter and voltmeter to measure the lamp current and potential difference.
ms: Ammeter in series with lamp (1).
Voltmeter in parallel across lamp (1).

parts.q: State what current is and what potential difference measures.
ms: Current is the rate of flow of charge (1).
Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge (1).

questions.title: Resistance in circuits
questions.stem: Two resistors of 4 Ω and 8 Ω are connected in series to a 6.0 V supply. Use R = V/I.

parts.q: Calculate the total resistance.
ms: Series resistances add: 4 + 8 (1).

parts.q: Calculate the current from the supply.
Calculate the potential difference across the 8 Ω resistor.
Compare this series circuit with connecting the resistors in parallel to the same supply.
ms: Each parallel branch has full 6.0 V (1).
Total parallel resistance is less than either individual resistance (1).
Total supply current is greater in parallel (1).

questions.title: Particles and changes of state
questions.stem: A metal block has mass 540 g and volume 200 cm³. A separate sample of ice has mass 0.20 kg. Its specific latent heat of fusion is 330000 J/kg. Use density = mass/volume and E = mL.

parts.q: Calculate the density of the metal block.
Calculate the energy needed to melt all the ice at its melting point.
Explain why temperature stays constant while ice melts, although energy is transferred to it.
ms: Energy increases internal energy (1).
Used to overcome forces/bonds between particles rather than increase kinetic energy (1).
Temperature measures average particle kinetic energy, so it does not rise (1).

parts.q: Compare particle arrangements and motion in a solid and a gas.
ms: Solid particles close together in fixed/regular arrangement; gas particles far apart/random (1).
Solid particles vibrate about fixed positions (1).
Gas particles move rapidly in random directions (1).

questions.title: Radiation and half-life
questions.stem: A radioactive source has background-corrected count rate 160 counts/s. Its half-life is 4 hours.

parts.q: Calculate the count rate after 12 hours.
ms: 12/4 = 3 half-lives (1).
20 counts/s (1).

parts.q: A detector records 65 counts/s near another source and 15 counts/s without it. Calculate the corrected source count rate.
ms: 50 counts/s (1).

parts.q: Compare the penetration of alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
ms: Alpha stopped by paper/skin/few cm of air (1).
Beta stopped by thin aluminium (1).
Gamma most penetrating; intensity reduced by thick lead/concrete (1).

parts.q: Explain why irradiation does not necessarily make an object radioactive.
ms: Irradiation is exposure to radiation from an external source (1).
No radioactive material has necessarily been transferred to the object (1).

questions.title: Electricity at home
questions.stem: A 2.0 kW kettle runs for 3 minutes. Electricity costs 30 pence per kWh. Use energy in kWh = power in kW × time in hours.

parts.q: Calculate the electrical energy used in kWh.
Calculate the cost of using the kettle once.
ms: 3.0 pence (1).

parts.q: Explain how an earth wire and fuse protect someone if a live wire touches a metal case.
ms: Earth provides low-resistance path to ground (1).
Large fault current flows (1).
Fuse melts/breaks circuit so case is disconnected from live supply (1).

parts.q: State the approximate UK mains potential difference and frequency.

questions.title: Energy and efficiency
questions.stem: A 120 kg trolley starts from rest and descends 5.0 m. It reaches 8.0 m/s. Take g = 9.8 N/kg. Use Eₚ = mgh and Eₖ = 0.5mv².

parts.q: Calculate the decrease in gravitational potential energy.
Calculate the kinetic energy at the bottom.
Calculate the percentage of the lost gravitational potential energy transferred to kinetic energy.
ms: Efficiency = useful/total (1).

parts.q: Explain why the trolley speed is lower than predicted by a model with no friction.
ms: Friction/air resistance do work (1).
Energy transferred to thermal stores of trolley/track/air (1).
Less of the gravitational potential energy is available as kinetic energy; total energy still conserved (1).

questions.title: Measuring specific heat capacity
questions.stem: An insulated 0.80 kg metal block is heated by a 24 W heater for 300 s. Its temperature rises by 10.0 °C. Use E = Pt and E = mcΔθ.

parts.q: Calculate the electrical energy supplied.
Calculate the experimental specific heat capacity.
Explain how energy loss to the surroundings affects this calculated value.
ms: Some supplied energy does not heat the block (1).
Measured temperature rise is smaller than without losses (1).
Using all supplied energy in E/(mΔθ) makes calculated c too high (1).

parts.q: Suggest two practical steps to reduce this error.
ms: Improve insulation/use a lid (1).
Good heater/thermometer contact with block using oil in holes, or start below room temperature and end equally above it (1).

questions.title: Electrical networks
questions.stem: A 6 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across an ideal 12 V supply. Use V = IR and P = VI.

parts.q: Calculate the current in each branch.
ms: Both branches have 12 V (1).

parts.q: Calculate the total resistance of the combination.
ms: Total current = 2.0 + 1.0 = 3.0 A (1).

parts.q: Calculate the total power transferred.
Explain why adding another parallel resistor increases the current supplied.
ms: Adds another path for charge so total resistance decreases (1).
At fixed supply potential difference, lower resistance means greater total current (1).

questions.title: Resistance, temperature and safety
questions.stem: A 230 V heater transfers 1840 W. Use P = VI. A student also investigates a filament lamp using a variable supply.

parts.q: Calculate the normal operating current of the heater.
Choose the smallest suitable fuse from 3 A, 5 A and 13 A and justify the choice.
ms: Above normal current so it does not melt in normal use, but breaks circuit at excessive current (1).

parts.q: Describe a safe investigation of the current-potential difference characteristic of a filament lamp. Explain the shape expected and how to check both current directions.
ms: Connect lamp, variable low-voltage supply/variable resistor and ammeter in series, with voltmeter in parallel across lamp.
Vary potential difference in small steps and record pairs of current and potential difference.
Reverse supply connections to obtain readings for the opposite direction; repeat readings where needed.
Limit current/voltage to safe lamp ratings and avoid touching a hot filament bulb.
Plot current against potential difference: curve becomes less steep as the magnitude of potential difference increases.
Higher current heats the filament; increased ion vibrations cause more electron collisions, so resistance increases.
parts.note: Award one mark per distinct valid linked point, maximum 6.

questions.title: Latent heat and the particle model
questions.stem: A heater of power 60 W melts 0.18 kg of ice at 0 °C in 1100 s. In the model, all supplied energy melts the ice. Use E = Pt and E = mL.

parts.q: Calculate the experimental specific latent heat of fusion.
Explain why including energy used to warm the container would bias this value.
ms: Not all supplied energy melts ice (1).
Dividing total energy by melted mass overestimates true latent heat (1).

parts.q: Explain the constant temperature during melting using kinetic energy and potential energy.
ms: Internal energy increases (1).
Energy raises particle potential energy/overcomes interactions rather than raising average kinetic energy (1).
Average kinetic energy/temperature therefore remains constant (1).

parts.q: Explain why gas pressure rises when a gas is heated in a sealed rigid container.
ms: Particles move faster and collide more often/more forcefully with walls (1).
Greater total force on a fixed area increases pressure (1).

questions.title: Nuclear changes and half-life
questions.stem: A source gives 820 counts/min initially, including background of 20 counts/min. After 18 hours the total count rate is 120 counts/min.

parts.q: Determine the half-life of the source.
ms: Initial corrected count = 800 counts/min (1).
Final corrected count = 100 counts/min (1).

parts.q: A nucleus has atomic number 84 and mass number 212. State the atomic and mass numbers after alpha decay.
ms: Atomic number 82 (1).
Mass number 208 (1).

parts.q: Describe the changes in a nucleus during beta-minus decay.
ms: A neutron changes into a proton (1).
An electron/beta particle is emitted; atomic number rises by 1 and mass number unchanged (1).

parts.q: Explain why a precise decay time cannot be assigned to an individual nucleus.
ms: Radioactive decay is random/spontaneous (1).
Half-life predicts a statistical pattern for many nuclei, not when a particular nucleus decays (1).

questions.title: Generating electricity and national supply
questions.stem: A wind turbine transfers 1.8 MJ of useful electrical energy in 30 s. The energy transferred from wind during that time is 4.5 MJ.

parts.q: Calculate the useful electrical power in kW.
Calculate the efficiency as a decimal.
Explain why the National Grid transmits electricity at high potential difference.
ms: For a given power, higher voltage means lower current (1).
Lower current causes less heating/energy loss in transmission wires (1).
Makes transfer over long distances more efficient (1).

parts.q: Evaluate one advantage and one limitation of wind power compared with gas-fired generation.
ms: Renewable/no fuel combustion emissions during operation (1).
Intermittent output depends on wind, whereas gas generation is controllable; credit another correctly compared limitation (1).

questions.title: Motion of a cyclist
questions.stem: A cyclist travels 240 m in 40 s at constant speed, then speeds up from 6 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 s. Use speed = distance/time and a = (v-u)/t.

parts.q: Calculate the initial constant speed.
Calculate the acceleration during the next 4 s.
ms: Change in velocity = 10 - 6 = 4 m/s (1).

parts.q: Describe the appearance of a distance–time graph during the initial constant-speed motion.
ms: Straight line (1).
Constant positive gradient (1).

parts.q: Explain what happens to speed when the forward driving force equals the total resistive force.
ms: Resultant force is zero (1).
No acceleration (1).
Cyclist continues at constant speed in a straight line (1).

questions.title: Forces on a lift
questions.stem: A package has mass 12 kg. Take g = 10 N/kg. Two horizontal forces act on a different trolley: 80 N right and 35 N left. Use W = mg.

parts.q: Calculate the weight of the package.
Calculate the resultant horizontal force on the trolley and state its direction.
ms: To the right (1).

parts.q: Explain the difference between mass and weight.
ms: Mass is amount of matter; measured in kg (1).
Weight is gravitational force; measured in N (1).
Weight changes with gravitational field strength but mass does not (1).

parts.q: Name one contact force and one non-contact force.
ms: Friction/air resistance/tension/normal contact force (1).
Gravitational/electrostatic/magnetic force (1).

questions.title: Stretching springs
questions.stem: A spring extends by 0.040 m when a force of 8.0 N is applied. It has not passed its limit of proportionality. Use F = ke and E = 0.5ke².

parts.q: Calculate the spring constant.
Calculate the elastic potential energy stored.
ms: Extension squared = 0.0016 m² (1).

parts.q: State what is meant by elastic deformation.
ms: Object changes shape when force applied (1).
Returns to its original shape when force removed (1).

parts.q: Describe how a force–extension graph changes beyond the limit of proportionality.
ms: No longer a straight line through the origin (1).
Force is no longer directly proportional to extension (1).

questions.title: Water waves
questions.stem: A wave has frequency 5.0 Hz and wavelength 0.24 m. Use v = fλ and T = 1/f.

parts.q: Calculate the wave speed.
Calculate the period.
Explain the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves.
ms: In transverse waves oscillations are perpendicular to energy transfer (1).
In longitudinal waves oscillations are parallel (1).
Valid examples: electromagnetic/water waves transverse and sound longitudinal (1).

parts.q: Describe how to measure wavelength accurately in a ripple tank.
ms: Freeze pattern using strobe/photograph or project onto a screen (1).
Measure distance across several complete wavelengths (1).
Divide by number of wavelengths to reduce percentage measurement error (1).

questions.title: Electromagnetic radiation
questions.stem: Electromagnetic waves travel at 300000000 m/s in a vacuum. A radio wave has frequency 100000000 Hz. Use v = fλ.

parts.q: Calculate the radio wavelength.
Put infrared, ultraviolet, radio and visible light in increasing order of frequency.
ms: Radio before infrared (1).
Infrared before visible (1).
Visible before ultraviolet, giving radio → infrared → visible → ultraviolet (1).

parts.q: Give one use and one hazard of ultraviolet radiation.
ms: Security marking/fluorescent lamps/sterilisation (1).
Skin damage/skin cancer/eye damage (1).

parts.q: State two features shared by all electromagnetic waves.
ms: Transverse waves (1).
Same speed in vacuum/can transfer energy through vacuum (a second valid feature for 1).

questions.title: Measuring waves on a string
questions.stem: A vibrator produces waves along a string. The wavelength is measured as 0.80 m and the frequency is 12 Hz. Use v = fλ.

parts.q: Calculate the wave speed.
State why measuring across several wavelengths is better than measuring one.
ms: Reduces relative/percentage uncertainty in total length (1).
Dividing the length by number of wavelengths gives a better estimate of mean wavelength (1).

parts.q: Describe a safe method to investigate how changing frequency affects wavelength when wave speed is kept approximately constant.
ms: Use a vibrator connected to a signal generator with a string under fixed tension.
Keep the same string and tension/attached load for all readings.
Set and record a range of frequencies from the signal generator.
Measure a clearly defined distance across several wavelengths using a ruler.
Divide measured distance by number of wavelengths, repeat and calculate mean wavelength.
Keep electrical apparatus dry/secure the apparatus and prevent falling masses; compare fλ values or plot wavelength against frequency. Safety must be included for full 6 marks.
parts.note: Award one mark per distinct valid point, maximum 6.

questions.title: Magnets and electromagnets
questions.stem: A coil of insulated wire is wrapped around an iron nail and connected to a low-voltage supply.

parts.q: State how magnetic field lines are directed outside a bar magnet and where the field is strongest.
ms: From north pole to south pole (1).
Strongest near poles/where lines are closest (1).

parts.q: Describe how a compass can be used to plot a magnetic field.
ms: Place compass at a point and mark needle direction (1).
Move along that direction and repeat to form a field line (1).
Repeat from different starting positions and add arrows (1).

parts.q: Describe three factors that affect the strength of an electromagnet.
ms: A larger current, within safe limits, makes it stronger (1).
More turns in the coil make it stronger (1).
A soft iron core makes the field stronger than the same coil without a core (1).

parts.q: Explain why an electromagnet is useful in a scrapyard crane.
ms: Can attract/lift iron or steel objects (1).
Can be switched off to release them (1).

questions.title: Acceleration and force
questions.stem: A 950 kg car accelerates uniformly from 8.0 m/s to 20.0 m/s in 6.0 s. Use a = (v-u)/t, F = ma and distance = average speed × time for uniform acceleration.

parts.q: Calculate the acceleration.
Calculate the resultant force.
Calculate the distance travelled during the acceleration.
ms: Distance = 14.0 x 6.0 (1).

parts.q: Explain how increasing passenger mass affects acceleration if the same resultant force acts.
ms: Total mass increases (1).
Acceleration decreases in inverse proportion to mass at constant force (1).

questions.title: Stopping a vehicle
questions.stem: A driver travels at 24 m/s. Their reaction time is 0.75 s. Braking then reduces speed uniformly to zero over 48 m. Use distance = speed × time for thinking distance and v² - u² = 2as for braking.

parts.q: Calculate the thinking distance.
Calculate the magnitude of the deceleration during braking.
ms: Magnitude = 6.0 m/s² (1).

parts.q: Calculate total stopping distance.
Explain one factor affecting thinking distance and one affecting braking distance.
ms: Alcohol/tiredness/distraction increases reaction time (1).
So thinking distance increases at the same speed (1).
Wet/icy roads reduce friction, increasing braking distance, or worn brakes/tyres reduce braking force (1).

questions.title: Momentum in a collision
questions.stem: A 0.80 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m/s collides with a stationary 1.20 kg trolley. They join together. External horizontal forces are negligible. Use p = mv.

parts.q: Calculate the total momentum before collision.
Calculate the common speed after collision.
ms: Momentum is conserved (1).
Combined mass = 2.00 kg and v = 2.40/2.00 (1).

parts.q: Explain why momentum conservation does not mean kinetic energy must also be conserved in this collision.
ms: Momentum is conserved for an isolated system/no external resultant force (1).
Joining/deformation transfers some kinetic energy to thermal/internal stores and sound (1).
Total energy conserved, but kinetic energy after collision is lower (1).

parts.q: Explain, using acceleration and force, why a car crumple zone reduces force on passengers in a crash.
ms: Increases stopping time/distance, reducing deceleration for the same velocity change (1).
F = ma: lower magnitude of acceleration means lower force for the same mass (1).

questions.title: Wave speed and refraction
questions.stem: A wave of frequency 8.0 Hz travels in deep water at 2.4 m/s, then enters shallow water where speed is 1.6 m/s. Use v = fλ.

parts.q: Calculate its wavelength in deep water.
Calculate its wavelength in shallow water.
ms: Frequency remains 8.0 Hz, so λ = 1.6/8.0 (1).

parts.q: Explain why the wave changes direction when it enters shallow water at an angle.
ms: Wave speed decreases (1).
Part of wavefront enters shallow water and slows before the rest (1).
Wave bends towards the normal (1).

parts.q: Describe how to measure the speed of ripples experimentally.
ms: Measure wavelength over several waves and divide (1).
Measure frequency from number passing a point per measured time (1).
Calculate speed fλ; repeat measurements to reduce random uncertainty (1).

questions.title: Radiation and communication
questions.stem: A microwave link operates at 6.0 × 10⁹ Hz. Electromagnetic wave speed in air is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Use v = fλ.

parts.q: Calculate the microwave wavelength.
Explain why electromagnetic waves can communicate with a satellite through space but sound cannot.
ms: Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum (1).
Sound is a mechanical wave and needs particles/a medium (1).

parts.q: Explain why X-rays can be more hazardous to living tissue than microwaves.
ms: X-rays are higher-frequency radiation (1).
Can ionise atoms/molecules and damage DNA/cells (1).
May cause mutations/cancer; microwaves principally cause heating at sufficiently high intensity (1).

parts.q: State a use of infrared and explain a related hazard.
ms: Thermal imaging/remote control/electrical heating (one valid use for 1).
Absorption can heat tissue/cause burns (1).

questions.title: Force on a current-carrying conductor
questions.stem: A straight wire of length 0.12 m lies perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.25 T. Current is 3.0 A. Use F = BIl.

parts.q: Calculate the force on the wire.
ms: Correct multiplication (1).

parts.q: Explain the effect of reversing the current and of reversing both current and field.
ms: Reversing current alone reverses force (1).
Reversing field alone also reverses force (1).
Reversing both leaves original force direction unchanged (1).

parts.q: State the direction of force relative to the field and current.
ms: Perpendicular to magnetic field (1).
Perpendicular to current (1).

parts.q: Explain why the wire has no motor-effect force when it is parallel to the field.
ms: Force depends on component of current/length perpendicular to field (1).
For parallel alignment this component is zero (1).

questions.title: Investigating a spring
questions.stem: A spring obeys F = ke up to 6.0 N. Its extension at 6.0 N is 0.030 m. Use E = 0.5ke².

parts.q: Calculate the energy stored at 6.0 N.
Design an investigation to determine the spring constant and identify the limit of proportionality. Include measurements, processing and safety.
ms: Clamp spring securely next to a vertical ruler and measure unloaded length.
Add known weights in small increments and allow spring to settle.
Measure loaded length at eye level and calculate extension by subtraction.
Repeat readings/unload to check reproducibility and whether original length is recovered.
Plot force against extension; gradient of initial straight-line region gives k and departure marks limit of proportionality.
Secure stand/use eye protection and prevent masses falling on feet; avoid excessive loads. Safety must be included for full 6 marks.
parts.note: Award one mark per distinct valid linked point, maximum 6.
